meta.description: Not original to MLK — it's Amos 5:24. King made the verse famous in 1963, but the words are Scripture (KJV: "let judgment run down as waters").
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Justice runs down like water, and righteousness like a mighty stream'?
meta.ogDescription: Not MLK's own words — it's the prophet Amos (Amos 5:24). King borrowed and popularized the verse in his 1963 "I Have a Dream" speech.

answer.label: Not Martin Luther King Jr. — it’s the prophet Amos
answer.authorDates: 8th century BC · Hebrew prophet, Book of Amos
answer.sourceLine: These are the words of the prophet Amos, from Amos 5:24. The King James rendering reads “But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream” — the source of the “runs down like water…mighty stream” phrasing. Martin Luther King Jr. did not originate this line; he quoted and popularized it, most famously at the 1963 March on Washington, where his own wording was “justice rolls down like waters, and righteousness like a mighty stream.” The words are Scripture, so crediting them to King as their author is a misattribution.

source.excerpt: Take thou away from me the noise of thy songs; for I will not hear the melody of thy viols. But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.
trail: The words are Scripture: Amos 5:24. The King James Version reads “But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream” (Bible Hub ↗).

Martin Luther King Jr. made the verse famous by paraphrasing it in his 1963 “I Have a Dream” speech — “we will not be satisfied until justice rolls down like waters and righteousness like a mighty stream” (HistoryNet transcript ↗).

The specific “runs down like water…mighty stream” wording tracks the KJV (“run down as waters…mighty stream”) and ASV (“justice roll down as waters…mighty stream”) — not King’s own “rolls down like waters” phrasing (translation comparison ↗).
source.excerptNote: Amos 5:23–24, King James Version (1611). The American Standard Version (1901) renders it “But let justice roll down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.”
source.rightsNote: The line is Amos 5:24 from the Hebrew Bible, an ancient text. The renderings that carry this exact language — the King James Version (1611, “let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream”) and the American Standard Version (1901) — are both firmly in the public domain, and the modernized “justice runs down like water” wording derives from that public-domain text.

author.name: Amos
author.heading: Amos, prophet of Tekoa
author.metaLine: 8th century BC · Hebrew prophet & shepherd of Tekoa
author.bio: Amos was a herdsman and fig-grower from Tekoa in Judah who prophesied in the northern kingdom of Israel around 760–750 BC, making him among the earliest of the literary prophets. His short book denounces empty ritual and social injustice, culminating in the demand of Amos 5:24 that justice and righteousness flow like unstoppable water. The verse became a rallying cry of the American civil-rights movement through Martin Luther King Jr., who quoted it repeatedly.

misattribution.heading: Why it’s pinned on MLK
misattribution.intro: Because Martin Luther King Jr. quoted Amos 5:24 so powerfully and so often, the line is now routinely captioned as though he composed it. He didn’t — he was quoting the Bible.

items.why: King quoted the verse throughout his ministry and made it iconic at the 1963 March on Washington, but his own wording was “justice rolls down like waters” — a paraphrase of Amos, not an original composition (speech transcript ↗).

items.who: The King James / American Standard Version
items.why: “Runs down like water…mighty stream” matches the KJV (“judgment run down as waters…a mighty stream”) and ASV (“justice roll down as waters…a mighty stream”), not King’s spoken text (Bible Hub ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The words belong to the prophet Amos (Amos 5:24 ↗); Martin Luther King Jr. borrowed and immortalized them, but did not write them.

context.heading: An ancient line, a modern movement
lead: Amos 5:24 sits at the heart of the prophet’s attack on hollow worship: God rejects Israel’s festivals and songs and demands instead that justice and righteousness pour out like water that cannot be dammed. It is one of the oldest and starkest statements of social justice in Western scripture.

Martin Luther King Jr. returned to the verse again and again — in the 1963 “I Have a Dream” speech, in letters and sermons — until it became fused with his own voice. Maya Lin later carved King’s rendering into the Civil Rights Memorial in Montgomery. The fusion is why the line is now so often miscredited to King as its author.
context.pull: Let justice roll down like waters — the prophet’s demand, the preacher’s refrain.
